common_name: Dragon's Breath Pepper (Extreme Ornamental Superhot Chile)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since Capsicum chinense germinates slowly; transplant only after nights stay reliably above 55F, since this is one of the slowest-fruiting chiles to mature.

directions: Dragon's Breath was bred in Wales through a collaborative trial investigating the essential oil's potential as a topical anesthetic, and it produces small, wrinkled, roughly one-inch fruits on a compact, well-branched plant that suits container growing as easily as garden beds. Independent lab testing reported an extraordinary capsaicin concentration around 2.48 million Scoville units, though this figure has not been formally certified, so treat it as a claimed rather than official record. Because of its almost unmanageable heat, growers treat the fruit as a novelty or oil-extraction crop rather than a table pepper, and any handling should be done with gloves, eye protection, and excellent ventilation. Give plants the same warm, sunny, well-drained conditions used for habaneros, and expect a long season since fruit set and full ripening take considerably longer than most annuum peppers.
sources: Nottingham Trent University research announcements on Dragon's Breath essential oil
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; NuMex Easter is a compact, early-maturing ornamental well suited to patio containers and hanging baskets as well as garden beds.

directions: NuMex Easter was released by the New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute and named a 2014 All-America Selections winner for its striking clusters of small, upright, teardrop-shaped fruit that shift through pastel lavender, cream, and yellow before finishing bright orange, often showing several colors on the same compact plant at once. The dense, fasciculate fruiting habit and dwarf stature, typically under a foot tall and about as wide, make it one of the most reliable ornamental peppers for small containers, window boxes, or mixed spring bedding displays. The fruit carries real heat, roughly in the cayenne-to-habanero range, and is technically edible, but it is grown almost exclusively for its ever-changing color display rather than culinary use. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and light monthly feeding to keep fruit set continuous through the season.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Espanola Improved Chile (Short-Season High-Altitude New Mexico Red Chile)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Espanola Improved was specifically bred for the short, cool growing season of north-central New Mexico's high-altitude valleys, so it reaches usable green-chile size faster than most New Mexico types and suits gardeners in shorter-season northern or high-elevation regions.

directions: Espanola Improved was released by New Mexico State University in 1984 as an early-maturing red chile bred for the shorter growing season and higher elevation of the Espanola Valley north of Santa Fe, where standard New Mexico chiles often fail to reach full red maturity before fall frost. The medium-length, tapered pods carry mild-to-medium heat and are traditionally harvested green for roasting or left on the plant to ripen fully red for the dried red chile ristras the region is known for. Compared to longer-season New Mexico cultivars, Espanola Improved sets fruit earlier and matures its red crop reliably even where the frost-free window is tight, making it a good choice for gardeners at altitude or in northern climates who still want authentic New Mexico chile flavor. Provide full sun, even moisture, and a warm start, since fruit set benefits from getting plants established as early as safely possible after the last frost.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Gernika Pepper (Basque Pimiento de Gernika Frying Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Gernika peppers are harvested young and green, well before full ripening, so successive picking every few days over a long season keeps plants productive.

directions: Gernika (Gernikako Piperra) is a slender, thin-walled sweet frying pepper protected under Spain's Denominacion de Origen Protegida in the Basque Country, where it is a signature tapas ingredient traditionally flash-fried whole in olive oil and finished with coarse salt. Pods are harvested small and immature, typically 2.5 to 3.5 inches long, while still green, since the variety is never grown to full ripeness for market; frequent harvesting at this young stage also keeps the compact plants setting new fruit continuously through summer. The thin flesh cooks in under a minute in hot oil, blistering the skin while the interior stays tender, with a flavor that is mild and sweet with only an occasional peppery bite from scattered hotter individual fruits, similar to Spain's Padron pepper but generally milder and more consistent. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and a support stake or cage for the heavily branched, fruit-laden plants.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Basque pepper variety documentation

common_name: Nora Pepper (Dried Spanish Sweet Pepper for Romesco)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Nora fruit must be left on the plant until fully red and wrinkled before harvest, since it is grown exclusively for drying rather than fresh eating, so plan for a full-length warm season.

directions: Nora is a small, round, thick-fleshed sweet pepper grown mainly in Murcia and Valencia in eastern Spain, where the deep red, fully ripe fruit is sun-dried whole rather than ground into powder, giving it a distinctively wrinkled, tomato-like appearance in the kitchen. Its heat is negligible, well under 1,000 Scoville units, so its value lies entirely in a sweet, earthy, almost raisin-like dried flavor that develops through slow drying and forms the flavor backbone of romesco sauce, arroz negro, and many Murcian and Valencian braises and rice dishes. Fruit should be harvested only after turning fully red and slightly soft, then air-dried or dehydrated over several weeks until the skin is leathery and the pepper rattles faintly with loose seeds, similar in method to the Mexican cascabel. Because Nora needs a long season to reach full red ripeness, gardeners outside mild climates should start plants early and grow them in the warmest, sunniest spot available.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Spanish dried pepper variety documentation

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since this is a slow-germinating, slow-maturing superhot that needs a long warm season to fully ripen its fruit.

directions: 7 Pot Jonah is a Trinidad-origin strain of the 7 Pot family, producing bumpy, elongated pods that ripen from green to a distinctive pale, almost bone-white to light-yellow or pinkish color rather than the deep red typical of most 7 Pot types. Heat runs from roughly 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville units, placing it firmly among the world's hottest cultivated peppers alongside Douglah and Primo, but it is prized among chileheads for a sweet, fruity flavor that comes through despite the intensity. Plants grow tall and vigorous for a Capsicum chinense, often exceeding three feet, and benefit from staking once heavily laden with fruit. Always wear gloves when harvesting or processing ripe pods, and keep hands away from eyes and face.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Explosive Ember Pepper (Purple-Foliage Ornamental Hot Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; Explosive Ember is bred for compact hanging baskets and containers as much as garden beds.

directions: Explosive Ember is an ornamental pepper bred as a companion to the popular Black Pearl variety, distinguished by bright purple young foliage and white-and-purple flowers rather than Black Pearl's near-black leaves. Its slender, upright, conical fruit emerges a vivid neon purple and ripens through orange to red, often showing all three colors in the same cluster for a long-lasting, ever-changing display. The fruit carries genuine heat in the tabasco-to-cayenne range, roughly 30,000 Scoville units, and while technically edible it is grown almost entirely for ornamental impact in beds, containers, and hanging baskets. Plants stay compact and well-branched without pinching, tolerate summer heat well, and continue setting new fruit clusters over a long season with routine watering and light monthly feeding.
sources: Proven Winners — Capsicum ornamental pepper series descriptions
